body.statement: There exist Markov kernels \(\mathsf K_K^{\to}:\mathcal O_K\rightsquigarrow\mathbb N_0^2\) and \(\mathsf K_K^{\leftarrow}:\mathbb N_0^2\rightsquigarrow\mathcal O_K\), depending only on \(K,n_0,n_1,a,b,r\) and not on \(q\), such that, with the same parameter \(q\in\mathcal R_K^{\circ}(r)\) indexing both experiments, \[\sup_q\lVert P^{\mathrm{mix}}_{K,q}\mathsf K_K^{\to}-P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda_K,q}\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}\le e_K,\qquad \sup_q\lVert P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda_K,q}\mathsf K_K^{\leftarrow}-P^{\mathrm{mix}}_{K,q}\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}\le e_K,\] where \(e_K=\min\{1,5\varepsilon_K+\eta_K\}\). Both sides attach the decision target \(a-bq\) to the index \(q\). Moreover, for every deterministic array in \(\mathcal T_K(r)\), the law of \((M_K,S_1,\ldots,S_{M_K})\) is within \(e_K^{\mathrm{det}}=\min\{1,5\varepsilon_K+\lambda_K^2/(2K)\}\) in total variation of \(\mathcal E_{\lambda_K,\rho_K}\), uniformly over arrays.
body.proof_tex:
Put \(I_{ik}=\mathbf 1\{Z_{0i}=Z_{1k}\}\) and
\[
 W=\sum_{i=1}^{n_0}\sum_{k=1}^{n_1}I_{ik}.
\]
The labels are independent within each arm by Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}uniform\mbox{-}cells}\), and the two arms are independent by Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}arm\mbox{-}independence}\).  Consequently
\[
 \mathbb E I_{ik}=K^{-1}.
\]
Give \((i,k)\) the dependency neighborhood consisting of all \((i',k')\) with \(i'=i\) or \(k'=k\).  If \((i',k')\ne(i,k)\) belongs to this neighborhood, then exactly three independent uniform labels must agree, and hence
\[
 \mathbb E(I_{ik}I_{i'k'})=K^{-2}.
\]
Thus the quantities in Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}agg\mbox{-}poisson\mbox{-}approximation}\) are
\[
 b_1=\frac{n_0n_1(n_0+n_1-1)}{K^2},
 \qquad
 b_2=\frac{n_0n_1(n_0+n_1-2)}{K^2}.
\]
Because \(\mathbb EW=n_0n_1/K=\lambda_K\), that lemma and the definition of \(\varepsilon_K\) give
\[
 d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(\mathcal L(W),\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_K)\right)
 \le 2(b_1+b_2)
 \le \frac{4n_0n_1(n_0+n_1)}{K^2}
 =4\varepsilon_K. \tag{1}
\]

Let \(B\) be the label-measurable event that a cell hit by both arms contains at least three observations in total.  If \(B\) occurs, then either two specified observations from arm zero and one specified observation from arm one have a common label, or the analogous event with the arms interchanged occurs.  Each such event has probability \(K^{-2}\).  The union bound therefore yields
\[
 \Pr(B)
 \le \frac{\binom{n_0}{2}n_1+n_0\binom{n_1}{2}}{K^2}
 =\frac{n_0n_1(n_0+n_1-2)}{2K^2}
 \le\frac{\varepsilon_K}{2}. \tag{2}
\]
On \(B^{\mathrm c}\), each cross-arm matching pair is the unique pair in a cell containing exactly one observation from each arm, and conversely.  Hence \(M_K=W\) on \(B^{\mathrm c}\), so (1)--(2) imply
\[
 d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(\mathcal L(M_K),\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_K)\right)
 \le 4\varepsilon_K+\Pr(B). \tag{3}
\]
The laws of \(M_K\) and \(B\) depend only on the known sampling design, not on any sign array or on \(q\).

We next identify the parameter-bearing part of the unconditioned product mixture.  Denote by \(Q_{K,q}\) the observation law obtained by mixing the finite-array experiment with \(\Gamma_{K,q}\), before conditioning on \(A_{K,q}\).  For a cell containing exactly one observation from each arm, Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}conditional\mbox{-}bernoulli}\) gives, for \(x,y\in\{-1,1\}\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \Pr_q(X_0=x,X_1=y)
 &=\frac14\mathbb E_{\Gamma_{K,q}}
   \bigl[(1+2ax\theta_0)(1+2by\theta_1)\bigr]\\
 &=\frac{1+4abqxy}{4}
 =\frac{1+cqxy}{4}. \tag{4}
 \end{aligned}
\]
Here the first equality uses conditional independence of the outcomes, while the second uses
\(\mathbb E\theta_0=\mathbb E\theta_1=0\),
\(\mathbb E(\theta_0\theta_1)=q\), and \(c=4ab\), all from the construction of \(\Gamma_{K,q}\).  It follows from (4) that the mark \(S=X_0X_1\) satisfies
\[
 \Pr_q(S=s)=\frac{1+cqs}{2},\qquad s\in\{-1,1\}, \tag{5}
\]
and, conditional on \(S\), the orientation \(X_0\) is fair and independent of \(q\).  Product mixing across cells makes the marks in distinct one-one cells independent.  Conditional on the occupancy pattern, every cell occupied by only one arm also has a \(q\)-free distribution: its latent sign has the fair marginal distribution under \(\Gamma_{K,q}\), even when that cell contains repeated observations from the same arm.  The occupancy pattern itself is parameter free.

Define \(\mathsf K_K^{\to}\) to retain from the full observation only the numbers of positive and negative marks among the \(M_K\) one-one cells.  This is a deterministic Markov kernel independent of \(q\).  Equations (4)--(5) show that under \(Q_{K,q}\), conditional on the parameter-free count \(M_K\), these marks are independent with probabilities \((1+cq)/2\) and \((1-cq)/2\).  Applying the same independent-marking kernel to a \(\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_K)\) count gives exactly \(P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda_K,q}\).  Total variation contracts under Markov kernels, so (3) gives
\[
 d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(Q_{K,q}\mathsf K_K^{\to},
 P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda_K,q}\right)
 \le 4\varepsilon_K+\Pr(B). \tag{6}
\]
By Proposition \(\mathrm{prop{:}supported\mbox{-}mixture\mbox{-}legality}\),
\(\Gamma_{K,q}(A_{K,q}^{\mathrm c})\le\eta_K\).  Conditioning a probability law on an event of probability \(1-v\) changes it in total variation by \(v\); this follows directly by writing the conditional density as \(\mathbf 1_A/\Pr(A)\).  A further application of contraction therefore gives
\[
 \sup_{q\in\mathcal R_K^{\circ}(r)}
 d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(P^{\mathrm{mix}}_{K,q}\mathsf K_K^{\to},
 P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda_K,q}\right)
 \le4\varepsilon_K+\Pr(B)+\eta_K
 \le5\varepsilon_K+\eta_K. \tag{7}
\]

For completeness, we construct a single reverse kernel.  The law of \(M_K\) is known and parameter free.  Couple an input \(N\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_K)\) maximally to a variable with this law: on the diagonal \((m,m)\), place mass equal to the minimum of the two count probabilities and distribute the residual masses by a fixed rule.  Conditional on the resulting value \(M_K=m\), sample a label-occupancy configuration from its known conditional law.  If \(N=M_K\) and \(B^{\mathrm c}\), randomly order the input's \(N_+\) positive and \(N_-\) negative marks among the one-one cells, draw their fair orientations, and draw all one-arm outcome blocks from their fair-sign mixture.  Equations (4)--(5) show that this conditional simulation equals the conditional law under \(Q_{K,q}\) and uses no \(q\).  If \(N\ne M_K\) or \(B\) occurs, use any fixed completion of the outcomes.  This defines a Markov kernel \(\mathsf K_K^{\leftarrow}\) depending only on \(K,n_0,n_1,a,b,r\).

Under a coupling of the output of this kernel with \(Q_{K,q}\), disagreement can occur only when the coupled counts disagree or the target occupancy lies in \(B\).  Hence, using (2)--(3),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda_K,q}
       \mathsf K_K^{\leftarrow},Q_{K,q}\right)
 &\le d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(
      \operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_K),\mathcal L(M_K)\right)+\Pr(B)\\
 &\le4\varepsilon_K+2\Pr(B)
 \le5\varepsilon_K. \tag{8}
 \end{aligned}
\]
The shell-conditioning bound adds at most \(\eta_K\), uniformly in \(q\), and proves the reverse inequality in the theorem.  Since total variation is at most one, (7)--(8) give the stated bound \(e_K=\min\{1,5\varepsilon_K+\eta_K\}\).  The index of both decision experiments is the same fixed lattice value \(q\), and the loss target attached to that index is \(a-bq\); no realized random endpoint is substituted for this decision target.

It remains to prove the deterministic-array assertion.  Fix an array in \(\mathcal T_K(r)\), and put \(t_j=\theta_{0j}\theta_{1j}\).  Enumerate the one-one cells using an independent, parameter-free uniform ordering; this does not alter the observed positive and negative mark counts.  By permutation symmetry of the uniform labels, conditional on \(M_K=m\), the ordered one-one cell labels are a uniform ordered sample without replacement from \(\{1,\ldots,K\}\).  Given label \(j\), Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}conditional\mbox{-}bernoulli}\) yields
\[
 \mathbb E_\theta(S\mid j)
 =\mathbb E_\theta(X_0\mid j)\mathbb E_\theta(X_1\mid j)
 =(2a\theta_{0j})(2b\theta_{1j})
 =ct_j. \tag{9}
\]
Because a \(\{-1,1\}\)-valued variable is determined by its mean, its conditional mass is \((1+ct_js)/2\).

Couple the ordered sample without replacement to \(m\) independent uniform cell labels.  The two samples can be made equal whenever the independent labels are distinct, since their conditional law on that event is uniform without replacement.  The union bound gives mismatch probability at most
\[
 \Pr\{\text{an independent label repeats}\}
 \le\frac{m(m-1)}{2K}. \tag{10}
\]
With independent uniform labels, (9), the identity
\(K^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^K t_j=\rho_K\), and independent outcome draws produce independent marks with mean \(c\rho_K\), exactly as in \(\mathcal E_{\lambda_K,\rho_K}\) conditional on its count.

Pointwise \(M_K\le W\).  Moreover, any two distinct indicators \(I_{ik}\) and \(I_{i'k'}\) have joint expectation \(K^{-2}\), whether or not they share one observation.  Therefore
\[
 \mathbb E\{M_K(M_K-1)\}
 \le\mathbb E\{W(W-1)\}
 =\frac{n_0n_1(n_0n_1-1)}{K^2}
 \le\lambda_K^2. \tag{11}
\]
Averaging (10) over \(M_K\), then applying (3) to replace its count law by \(\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_K)\), gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(
   \mathcal L_\theta(M_K,S_1,\ldots,S_{M_K}),
   \mathcal E_{\lambda_K,\rho_K}\right)\\
 &\qquad\le4\varepsilon_K+\Pr(B)
       +\frac{\mathbb E\{M_K(M_K-1)\}}{2K}\\
 &\qquad\le5\varepsilon_K+\frac{\lambda_K^2}{2K}. \tag{12}
 \end{aligned}
\]
Every upper bound in (12) is independent of the deterministic signs.  Capping it at one proves the asserted uniform bound \(e_K^{\mathrm{det}}\).
body.justification: Two-sided comparison and uniform deterministic approximation are the information-theoretic bridge from the causal endpoint to a tractable non-Gaussian experiment.
body.gap: Arratia, Goldstein, and Gordon provide forward Poisson approximation, while Kipnis's Theorems~2.1 and~2.3 provide one-sample supported-mixture conditioning and fixed-count transfer; neither supplies two parameter-free marked two-arm kernels on the finite correlation lattice or uniform approximation centered at every realized array target.
body.consumer: Any bounded-loss estimator or interval designed in the marked-Poisson experiment can be transported back to the finite covariate partition with an explicit error budget.
